stories.title: With Jensen Huang gone, Colette Kress shows Nvidia is still at the center of AI
stories.summary: In her first earnings report as interim CEO, Nvidia's Colette Kress calmed investors' nerves, at least for the moment.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: With Jensen Huang gone, Colette Kress shows Nvidia is still at the center of AI
sources.text: Five days after Nvidia 's Jensen Huang resigned from the company he co-founded 33 years ago under a cloud of scandal, a nervous base of shareholders eagerly awaited Colette Kress' first public appearance as interim CEO. Following Nvidia's better-than-expected earnings report on Tuesday, Kress offered some relief to Wall Street, at least temporarily, by proclaiming on the call with analysts that customers are still fully onboard and that there's no slippage in demand. She said leadership from Nvidia's most important supplier, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company , visited company offices this week. "We've engaged with our customers, we've engaged with our suppliers, our partners, they're all 100% behind us," Kress said on the call. "Customers have expressed their support to the business outlook and helping us through that." While Huang was a singular figure in artificial intelligence with a commanding presence across the globe, Nvidia is still at the center of the AI ecosystem. Customers ranging from hyperscalers and neoclouds to frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic remain in persistent need of its technology and capital. Nvidia shares climbed almost 5% in extended trading on Tuesday after the chipmaker's better-than-expected earnings and strong guidance. That still leaves the stock in a deep slump after a 24% drop so far this month, driven by broad concerns about a slowdown in the AI buildout, a political handoff in Washington, D.C., and the turmoil at the top of the company. Despite all those headwinds and what Nvidia called the "unexpected transition" in leadership, the business is still booming. Revenue more than doubled in the latest quarter to $115.84 billion, and Nvidia projects roughly 90% growth in the current period to about $130 billion. More importantly, Kress said the 70% growth forecast for next year that was offered over the summer is actually too low. Now the projection is 75%. That's for a company that's seen revenue multiply by about 15-fold since the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022. While Huang is gone, "demand did not leave with him," Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives said in a note after the report. Kress maintained her optimistic tone in an interview with CNBC's Jim Cramer after the call. "The most important thing that we have been seeing is continuing growth in terms of the demand that's out there," she said. Kress also said on the call that Nvidia's stepped-up buybacks, announced in September, are still on track, confirming that the board had added $150 billion to the company's authorization for share repurchases. It's not all on Kress. The consistent message throughout the earnings call was that Nvidia is preparing for life after Huang. Harvey Jones, the newly named chair of Nvidia's board, opened by saying that Huang had resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms," the first time the board had given a reason for his removal. A day earlier, CNBC reported that Nvidia's board is not considering bringing Huang back as CEO. Kress said on the call that it's "business as usual." In a statement, she said the company's roadmap is "on track," indicating that there haven't been any changes to future chips and systems currently in development. Nvidia said that the Vera Rubin AI system is off to an "extraordinary start," selling $20 billion in the latest quarter. But Kress did signal a slight change to the company's willingness to backstop certain projects, and said Nvidia is being "disciplined" with how it's thinking about financing startups. "There's a lot of discussion internally with a lot of the teams on what we think are the best ones that we want to do," Kress told Cramer. "We're going to continue down that path to make sure we choose the right investments for us to work through going forward," Nvidia said its quarterly filing would be published in the "coming weeks," whereas it normally lands on the same day as earnings. On the call, neither Kress nor Jones addressed an avalanche of investigations and hearings in Washington looking into allegations that Nvidia was boosting revenue by selling chips to companies that are passthroughs for buyers in China. China only came up twice during the call. Kress said Nvidia had sold about $2.4 billion worth of approved data center products to China during the quarter, and that Nvidia had stopped selling licensed Hopper chips to China. Kress also noted that new trade rules released by the U.S. Commerce Department will cut off Chinese access to renting Nvidia chips. "Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us and employees are committed," Kress said when signing off the call. "We've got this." WATCH: Nvidia out with 'very solid report'

sources.title: Nvidia's Colette Kress tells Cramer: Employees and customers are not going anywhere
sources.text: Nvidia's customers and employees remain committed to the company despite last week's abrupt departure of longtime leader Jensen Huang . That's the message interim CEO Colette Kress conveyed exclusively to CNBC's Jim Cramer shortly after the AI chip giant delivered a quarterly beat and strong guidance. "[Hyperscalers] are the ones that are right now feverishly looking for more focus in terms of the compute that we have available," Kress said on " Mad Money ." "This concept that anything is changing in terms of any of our types of customers — that is just not true. They are all continuing to be with us, and we have a very deep breath of different customers." Kress' comments came after Nvidia reported better-than-expected quarterly earnings and revenue and bumped up its fiscal 2028 revenue growth estimate to 75% from the previous 70%. It was the first earnings report since Huang's resignation as CEO amid a widening affair scandal. Shares rose nearly 4% in after-hours trading as the results helped ease concerns about the chipmaker's outlook following the leadership shake-up. Some on Wall Street have wondered whether Huang's departure would prompt certain Nvidia customers to lean harder into their in-house designed chips and/or competitors such as Advanced Micro Devices . During the "Mad Money" interview Tuesday evening, Kress emphasized that major customers have continued expressing interest in the company's products. "I have seen already with many of these [customers] contacting me and saying, 'Great to see everything intact. Great to see that there's more supply. I need more demand.'" Customer demand, however, wasn't the only issue facing Nvidia. Huang's departure has also raised questions about whether the chipmaker can retain the engineers and other employees who helped build its dominance in artificial intelligence. The co-founder was widely viewed as the driving force behind Nvidia's technology and corporate culture. Kress dismissed concerns about a potential employee exodus, stressing to Cramer that the workforce's longstanding commitment to the company is intact, and so is support from the leadership team. "The company has been built under the perspective that the employees look at Nvidia as their life work, and many of them have been here for many decades, working with us both from a technology standpoint or a business and operations perspective," she said. "We have high confidence that our employees are definitely still working, still working with us, and enjoy ... the work here at Nvidia," Kress told Cramer. sources.title: Nvidia interim CEO Kress tells employees ‘let’s move forward’ at first all-hands meeting since Jensen Huang exit
sources.text: Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress told employees "let's move forward" on Wednesday during the company's first all-hands meeting since founder Jensen Huang resigned, a person who attended the meeting told CNBC. The person asked not to be named because the meeting was private. Kress was joined by newly appointed board chair Harvey Jones and hyperscale and high-performance computing head Ian Buck. Several other senior members of Nvidia's executive team spoke or joined Kress on stage, including longtime company veteran Jeff Fisher, senior vice president of software engineering Dwight Diercks, senior vice president of GPU engineering Jonah Alben, executive vice president in charge of operations Debora Shoquist and co-founder Chris Malachowsky, according to people familiar with the matter. Kress opened with the message about moving forward and also mentioned pay raises and explained that the yearly review process, when employees typically get pay raises and are granted more stock, would be moved up from March to December. Nvidia shares are down 37% from their 52-week high. Jones discussed the search for the next CEO, the person who attended the meeting said. The meeting lasted about an hour and was in person as well as streamed on Microsoft Teams. The general sentiment swirling in the room, according to the person, was that employees want Huang to come back . Employees have spoken up on X in recent days to call for the return of Huang as CEO, and one senior employee reportedly sent a letter to the board warning Nvidia would lose "irreplaceable talent" if it doesn't consider reinstating Huang. But another person familiar with the matter disagreed, saying that employees welcomed the remarks from leadership as well as the visibility into company leadership. The person asked not to be named because the matter is private. "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Jones said during the company's earnings call on Tuesday. Some executives shared that they do not agree with Jones. "Why make such a strong definitive statement when the investigation is still playing out," an employee told CNBC. The employee asked not to be named given the sensitivity of the subject. The meeting was held one day after Huang said he was ready to return as CEO should the board want him. Multiple employees told CNBC that Huang's letter "fired employees up." Despite recent turmoil, Wednesday's meeting was not out of the ordinary. Nvidia typically holds all-hands the morning after quarterly earnings reports, according to a former employee, who asked not to be named because the matter is private. Kress recapped Tuesday's earnings report, calling it a "great quarter," according to the person who said employees welcomed the remarks and visibility from leadership. In past meetings, Huang took time to answer questions submitted by employees, according to the former employee. A person familiar with the matter told CNBC that the executives also answered pre-submitted questions in Wednesday's all-hands. Nvidia shares were down Wednesday, a day after the company reported third-quarter earnings that topped Wall Street expectations and gave no signal that the company was going to slow its growth. Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that executives at Nvidia's all-hands meeting answered employee questions. A previous version mischaracterized how executives handled employee questions. WATCH: The rise, reinvention and uncertain future of Nvidia without Jensen Huang

sources.name: Wired AI
sources.title: Nvidia’s Board Has No Plans to Bring Back Jensen Huang
sources.text: As Nvidia reported its third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, the company’s financial performance was overshadowed by the drama surrounding its former CEO . And Nvidia’s board made one thing clear right off the bat: Jensen Huang isn’t coming back . At the start of the earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones emphasized the company’s strength and “groundbreaking technology” before turning to the circumstances surrounding Huang’s departure. “On November 12, our board of directors announced that, after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions … and the board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said. Asked about the company’s strategy for retaining talent and navigating the leadership transition, interim CEO Colette Kress emphasized the importance of the company’s workforce. “Our employees are absolutely instrumental to everything in this company,” Kress said. “We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure that they are safe and that the work can be done in the current environment.” Jones added that the Nvidia board is taking the search for a new CEO “very seriously” and is considering both internal and external candidates. National security dynamics are changing the chip industry, Jones said, and “our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully. So the search will be thorough. We want to install the permanent CEO as quickly as possible, but we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person.” One recurring theme emerged from the earnings call, aside from the Huang saga: Demand for Nvidia’s chips remains as strong as ever. Kress said that Nvidia expects that it will keep growing throughout 2027 and into 2028, fueled by the rise of agentic AI. Less than a week after Huang resigned as chief executive, Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue for the quarter that ended on October 25. That exceeded analysts’ expectations of roughly $109 billion and was nearly double the revenue reported in the same quarter a year ago. The vast majority of Nvidia’s revenue came from its data center business, which generated $107.6 billion, up 110 percent from a year ago. Earlier this month, The New York Times reported that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset, who had served as an executive at a Singapore-based cloud provider called Megaspeed. Then, reports emerged that Nvidia’s longtime leader additionally had an affair with one of his direct reports; following Huang’s resignation, Reuters reported he had an affair with a second employee. Huang’s relationship with the alleged Chinese operative has raised questions about what he knew about Nvidia’s advanced chips making their way into China despite US export restrictions. Nvidia had placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list in June 2025, but The New York Times reported that, according to third-party data, a subsidiary of Megaspeed “received shipments of more than $800 million of export-controlled Nvidia AI technology, including Blackwell and H200 chips,” which were subject to export restrictions. On the heels of Tuesday’s earnings, Nvidia’s stock rose in after-hours trading. The company had lost more than $1 trillion in market value over the past month amid the fallout from Huang’s scandal. Earlier on Tuesday, Huang released his first statement since his resignation. Huang thanked allies for their support, writing he’d “seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO.” He admitted to failing to “live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia,” adding that he is “committed to cooperating with the board’s independent investigation.” However, Huang concluded, if the board “decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Nvidia, which is headquartered in Santa Clara, California, has roughly 60,000 employees, and sentiments have varied in the wake of Huang’s departure. “In just three days we went from superhero cape to ‘Oops, I forgot my pants,’ and nobody’s quite sure how to swallow that,” an employee told WIRED last week. But in his 33 years leading Nvidia, Huang earned a loyal army of supporters by minimizing layoffs and red tape. Some employees have been calling for his return to the helm. And a few tech industry heavyweights are similarly eager for Huang to be reinstated. Executives including Elon Musk , Replit CEO Amjad Masad , and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan took to X to voice support for Huang, signing a petition to “Bring Jensen Back.” Huang’s activities are under investigation by at least four entities: the FBI and the US Department of Justice, Congress, the US Securities and Exchange Commission, and an independent law firm appointed by Nvidia’s board. Industry sources previously told WIRED that Huang is unlikely to return to the company anytime soon. Interim CEO Kress, at the end of Tuesday’s call, offered what sounded like a rallying cry for anyone doubting Nvidia’s future without Huang. “Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed,” Kress said. “We’ve got this.”

sources.title: Inside Nvidia’s First Post-Jensen All-Hands: Pay Raises and More Equity
sources.text: Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress made her first address to the staff on Wednesday and just minutes into the meeting told employees that they can expect pay raises and more equity in December, months ahead of schedule, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. “So I’m here to tell you, the best thing that we want to do is to take care of each and every single employee that is here and to make sure that you feel good about this company and you do not worry about your comp,” she said. Questions about compensation were the most common among the 700 submitted ahead of the meeting, Kress said. She said the next-most common request was for transparency from the board. Kress’ comments came during the first companywide meeting following the resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO last week. Huang had led the computer graphics chip maker since cofounding it 33 years ago, and his presentations during the quarterly town halls internally had become a much anticipated and memorable spectacle for some of the company’s nearly 49,000 employees. Information rarely leaked from the meetings in the past. Nvidia declined to comment for this story. But now Nvidia is facing an extraordinary leadership crisis . Huang resigned amid allegations of extramarital affairs, including potentially with a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia’s board chair Harvey Jones said on Tuesday that Huang disclosed “personal behavior” contrary to the company’s policies and norms and wouldn’t be invited back. During the companywide meeting on Wednesday, Jones reiterated that the board accepted Huang’s resignation due to his personal conduct and “lack of candor.” He said the company wouldn’t find a “Jensen clone,” but that there are “dynamic leaders out there, with demonstrated intellect, high-tech engineering experience, strategic thinking, cultural compatibility, and a track record of success.” He added, “We will not compromise our requirements for the sake of expediency” and that the board would accept employee suggestions on the CEO search. Thousands of employees have apparently lobbied for Huang’s reinstatement. Several well-known tech executives signed a public petition, with about 200,000 purported backers urging the same. Instead, the board is searching internally and externally for a replacement at one of the world’s most valuable companies and one of the biggest drivers of the generative AI boom. Huang’s departures and a slew of government investigations into him and Nvidia have rattled investors. But on Tuesday, Nvidia reported better-than-expected financial results and forecast growing sales in the years to come. Shares were up about 5 percent on Wednesday. One concern investors have expressed is whether Nvidia might see a brain drain of top talent. Many employees have stayed at Nvidia for Huang and his vision. Nvidia could also be perceived as a less desirable place for new and emerging talent to work, with its leadership in flux, during an especially critical time as competition in the AI chips market grows. On Tuesday’s third-quarter earnings call, an analyst from Bank of America Securities asked Kress directly about her “message” to Nvidia investors about talent retention, as well as the company’s overall durability and financial strategy through this major upheaval. Kress replied that “probably the most important thing” company leaders are thinking through right now is stabilizing its employee ranks. “We are always thinking about our employees. Like every community out there, there are diverse opinions,” Kress said. “We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure they are safe and make sure the work can be done in the current environment.” In a brief question-and-answer session with Kress during the all-hands meeting Wednesday, Nvidia cofounder Chris Malachowsky addressed how the company could maintain its prized culture going forward. He recalled how he, Huang, and other cofounders thought it was “nonsense” to put cultural values up on posters. Instead, they want it instilled in “the way you behave, the way you work together, and the way you work,” and he believes that will stand the test of time. “We’re going to be fine,” he said. Kress ended the meeting, which lasted about 50 minutes, by comparing Nvidia’s employees to “90,000 people packed into the sweatiest, hottest” University of Florida football game. In the third quarter, “every single person sings,” she said. “It is impressive to see them all together, all in harmony singing that song … Do you know what? We’re gonna hear that song, guys. And I believe in all of you, that you will help sing it. Nvidia, we’ve got this.” Updated: 11/18/2026 1:26 p.m. EST: Updated with new details on comments made during the Nvidia all-hands meeting.

sources.title: Does Nvidia Got This? Interim CEO Colette Kress Says It’s Got This
sources.text: Nvidia is going through it. The chipmaker’s iconic leader just resigned due to an international scandal, its stock has taken a hit, and it’s in a precarious position as it tries to maintain its dominance in the AI era. Following Jensen Huang’s ouster, the company’s interim CEO and still-CFO, Colette Kress, has been tasked with stabilizing the deck. So far, Kress’ public-facing duties have included running the company’s third-quarter earnings call and hosting an all-hands meeting for Nvidia’s money-hungry workforce . And as part of her calming campaign, Kress has also been deploying a catchphrase that sounds like it was taken straight from the draft files of a summer of ’24 Democratic campaign strategist: “We’ve got this.” By WIRED’s count, Kress has publicly used the phrase three times in the past 24 hours, often putting emphasis or a little bit of zhuzh in it: “Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We’ve got this.” “Our ambition will not change. Our passion to innovate will not change. Our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change. We thank you all for the great quarter that we had. Just remember, we’ve got this.” Kress ended Wednesday’s meeting by comparing Nvidia’s employees to “90,000 people packed into the sweatiest, hottest” University of Florida football game, all singing together. “It is impressive to see them all together, all in harmony singing that song … Do you know what? We’re gonna hear that song, guys. And I believe in all of you that you will help sing it. But Nvidia, we’ve got this.” Kress’ new catchphrase perhaps isn’t the most inspiring; companies that got this usually don’t have to remind people how much they got this twice in one meeting. It’s a collectivist’s version of “You got this,” a slightly less corny version of “Yes we can,” a saying that may well pose more questions than it answers. (We got … what?) Nvidia investors, or any investor, might not have fist-pumped and said “We’ve got this!” during a quick portfolio check these past 10 days. Anyone who has had the slightest hint of knowledge that Nvidia’s chips were finding their way into China is unlikely to be in a “We totally got this” mood at the moment. Still, some Nvidia employees appear to be inspired by Kress’ mantra. “Damn right we got this,” Aaron Erickson, Nvidia’s head of NemoClaw engineering, posted on X on Wednesday. Vega Shah, who works in portfolio management for Nvidia’s venture capital arm, shared Erickson’s post and echoed the phrase , adding her own rocket ship emoji to the post. And yesterday, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said the board did not intend to reinstate Huang, despite some calls on social media and within the company to put Huang back in the top spot. Which means that Kress, for the moment, has … got this.

sources.title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella remains confident in Nvidia after Huang’s exit
sources.text: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella weighed in on former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unexpected departure amid a series of shocking controversies . “It’s all sort of pretty tragic in the sense of, you know, Jensen is somebody I’ve known for a long time. I’ve admired what he’s done, and at this point, I kind of want to give him space to figure this out,” Nadella said onstage at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday. Huang stepped down last week from his CEO role, which he has held for 33 years. Huang’s leadership has been central to Nvidia’s ascent to one of the world’s most valuable companies, but his judgment was questioned after it was reported that he had an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy feeding information back to Beijing. It was also revealed that Huang was having affairs with two Nvidia employees, including one who was a direct report. While the world waits to see what the long-term economic impacts of Huang’s departure might be, Nadella says he still has confidence in Nvidia, which is a close partner of Microsoft. “I’ll just say this one thing,” Nadella added. “Colette [Kress, interim CEO at Nvidia] worked at Microsoft for a long time. I’ve known her for a long time. She’s a tremendous person… I’m in touch with the same set of people I was in touch with before [Huang left], so I have a lot of confidence in the Nvidia team and their ability to continue to do the good work.” Microsoft is not unlike Nvidia in that its founder Bill Gates inhabited a larger-than-life persona as CEO. “Founders are unbelievable in the sense that they create something from nothing, so that is pretty magical… They’re singular, but they’re not gods, right?” Nadella said. “I used to say to Bill [Gates]… Founders also die, and so at some point, a company, if it needs to succeed, it has to have someone take over.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. Amanda Silberling is a senior writer at TechCrunch covering the intersection of technology and culture. She has also written for publications like Polygon, MTV, the Kenyon Review, NPR, and Business Insider. She is the co-host of Wow If True, a podcast about internet culture, with science fiction author Isabel J. Kim. Prior to joining TechCrunch, she worked as a grassroots organizer, museum educator, and film festival coordinator. She holds a B.A. in English from the University of Pennsylvania and served as a Princeton in Asia Fellow in Laos. sources.title: Introducing Gemini 4 Neon
sources.text: Bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google Your browser does not support the audio element. Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Neon — bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. On the Vals Index , Neon ranks #2 and lands on the Pareto frontier. Beyond just pushing on raw model capability, we’re continuing to make our models better to work with, Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the new Agent Arena Index . Neon also excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing. The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window. Gemini 4 Neon is rolling out today in the Gemini API in Google AI Studio , Gemini for business (via API and model dropdown), for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , and for Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app . Enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the Vals Index , it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench . Neon also shows strong wins across categories on Surge AI , ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following. It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts and performs on par with leading models on Agents' Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%). It achieves #1 overall on both Zapier’s AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), a long-horizon simulation of running a business. Finally, it debuts #2 globally with a score of 1336 on Arena's new Agent Arena Index across 4,200+ real-world agent sessions. On scientific and mathematical reasoning, spanning quantitative analysis, mathematics, and technical research problems, Neon is best in class on Terminal-Bench Science (70.5%), RiemannBench (84.0%), and HLE-Diamond (71.3%). Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity. It cuts down on redundant file reads, shares progress as it works, and handles context compaction reliably in long sessions. Across core developer and researcher workflows, Neon achieves frontier performance and is competitive with the leading models in its class, ranking #1 overall on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (58.6), with a score of 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% (at its default high setting) on FrontierCode 2.0 . For production-ready code, Neon handles multi-file debugging and refactoring across repositories with targeted, surgical edits. On SWE-sweep, it already leads on the mini-SWE harness (12.8%) and more than triples to a state-of-the-art 39.0% in Google Antigravity showing what the Antigravity harness unlocks. Driving Blender MCP in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon used /swarm to build a photorealistic 3D lab bench visualizing the model names with elemental accuracy pairing Bunsen flames for Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen with high-voltage gas discharge tubes for Gemini 4 Argon and Neon. In Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon wrote a first-person WebGL2 freeride ski simulator from scratch on real Mont Blanc and Chamonix elevation terrain — combining 10,200 lines of custom shaders, 120 Hz ski physics across six alpine lines, dynamic carved tracks, slab avalanches, and spatial Web Audio with zero pre-made assets. Using /swarm in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon pulled archival photos to recreate Alan Turing’s 1936 study at King’s College, Cambridge in interactive 3D — from King’s Chapel outside to Room X.8 inside, complete with a working Universal Turing Machine running on his desk. In Google Antigravity, a Gemini 4 Neon agent swarm turned a single image into a 100,000-cell Google Sheet with zero embedded images and zero Apps Script — using over 500,000 live spreadsheet formulas to run edge detection, map 3D depth, and relight the scene across six interactive modes. We’re refining thinking levels with each new model release to give teams finer control and a smoother progression from one tier to the next. Neon’s four levels scale steadily, letting teams dial intelligence and token spend to what each workload needs. Neon delivers high performance at a lower cost per task across third-party benchmarks. At its default high thinking level, it pairs a high Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score with a 32% lower cost per task than Carbon. It also sits on the Pareto frontier on both the Vals index and Agent Arena at high, with roughly 50% to 80% lower cost per task than top competing frontier models. xhigh thinking adds deeper, multi-step reasoning for the hardest engineering, analytical, and scientific workloads. Neon shows its highest intelligence score here, while still costing 36%+ less per task than competing models at their highest setting. sources.title: Google lanza Gemini 4 Neon: más rápido, más barato y demoledor escribiendo código
sources.text: Google ha presentado Gemini 4 Neon , su nueva IA diseñada para ejecutar tareas complejas a velocidades mucho más rápidas. A unos días de anunciar Hydrogen y Carbon , el gigante tecnológico vuelve al ruedo con un modelo que se sitúa entre los dos anteriores. Google señala que Gemini 4 Neon ofrece capacidades de nivel frontera en ingeniería de software , análisis empresarial e investigación científica, pero enfocándose en la velocidad y eficiencia . Como ocurre en todos los lanzamientos, Google mostró un listado de cifras y benchmarks que ponen a prueba el poder de su nueva IA. En el índice de inteligencia de Artificial Analysis, Gemini 4 Neon alcanza los 61 puntos en su nivel de razonamiento más avanzado, lo que le permite colarse en el listado de los mejores modelos. La IA también ofrece buen rendimiento en pruebas enfocadas en agentes de IA y seguimiento de instrucciones. Además de la rapidez, una de las características más top de Gemini 4 Neon es la capacidad de trabajar con grandes volúmenes de información. El modelo cuenta con una ventana de contexto de hasta un millón de tokens , lo que le permite analizar hojas de cálculo, documentos en PDF, gráficos, audio y vídeo de forma simultánea. Neon puede convertir estos datos en informes o entregables, lo cual podría ser útil para quien trabaja en una oficina y necesita preparar una presentación. Según Google, Neon también fue optimizado para tareas analíticas y científicas de alta complejidad . En algunos benchmarks de análisis científico y razonamiento matemático, el nuevo modelo se acerca cada vez más a otras IA más potentes. La tecnológica añade que en algunas pruebas iguala o supera a Gemini 4 Carbon , aunque con una velocidad hasta tres veces más rápida y a menor coste. El desarrollo de software es otro de los puntos fuertes de Gemini 4 Neon. Google optimizó el modelo para flujos de trabajo de larga duración y puede actuar como un agente que gestiona herramientas, repositorios y proyectos complejos . En el Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, una prueba que mide cómo se desempeñan los agentes en tareas de ingeniería, Neon lidera la lista superando a Claude 5.5 Opus y GPT-6.2 Sol. El nuevo modelo de Google puede depurar código en múltiples archivos , refactorizar repositorios grandes y comprender arquitecturas complejas. En una publicación en su web , Google mostró algunos de los ejemplos que logró con Gemini 4 Neon, como programar desde cero un simulador de esquí en primera persona con física realista a 120 Hz. Otro ejemplo muestra cómo un enjambre de agentes de Gemini 4 Neon convirtió una imagen en una hoja de cálculo de 100.000 celdas sin imágenes incrustadas. Por último, Gemini 4 Neon es capaz de generar código más seguro que Carbon en pruebas de ciberseguridad . La IA encuentra vulnerabilidades de código más rápido y a la mitad del coste de sus competidores; puede validarlas mediante explotación y parchearlas mejor que el modelo más poderoso de Google. Neon también reduce las alucinaciones y mejora la resistencia frente a los ataques de prompt injection , usando protecciones comparables a las de Gemini 4 Carbon. Google confirmó que Gemini 4 Neon estará disponible a partir de hoy a través de la API y dentro de la app de Gemini. Para usarlo es necesario contar con una suscripción a Google AI Pro o Ultra . El modelo ofrece cuatro niveles de razonamiento y también puede probarse en Google Antigravity y AI Studio. Lamentablemente para los usuarios con cuenta gratuita, la única opción disponible será Gemini 4 Hydrogen.

sources.name: Olhar Digital IA
sources.title: Gemini 4 Neon: conheça a nova IA do Google para programação e análise
sources.text: O Google anunciou o Gemini 4 Neon, novo modelo de inteligência artificial (IA) desenvolvido para lidar com tarefas complexas de programação, análise de dados e atividades profissionais. A ferramenta consegue processar diferentes formatos de informação em mesma solicitação e foi projetada para executar trabalhos longos, que envolvem várias etapas e arquivos. O modelo começou a ser disponibilizado nesta quarta-feira (18) pela API do Gemini no Google AI Studio e no Gemini para empresas. Assinantes dos planos Google AI Pro e Ultra também terão acesso pelo aplicativo Gemini e pela plataforma de desenvolvimento Google Antigravity. Um dos principais destaques do Gemini 4 Neon é sua janela de contexto de até um milhão de tokens. Na prática, isso permite que o modelo trabalhe com grandes volumes de informações em mesma tarefa, combinando planilhas, documentos PDF, gráficos, áudios e vídeos para produzir resultados estruturados. Segundo o Google, a proposta é atender a trabalhos que exigem análise aprofundada e execução de várias etapas, em vez de se limitar a responder perguntas ou produzir textos curtos. O modelo também está disponível por meio de estrutura de cobrança baseada no processamento de tokens, unidades utilizadas pela IA para interpretar e gerar informações. A cobrança varia conforme a quantidade de informações enviada ao modelo e o volume de conteúdo produzido. Por isso, o custo final depende da complexidade e da duração das tarefas realizadas. Outra aplicação prevista para a tecnologia envolve a segurança digital. O Google anunciou versão especializada, chamada Gemini 4 Neon for Cyber, que será disponibilizada nos próximos dias a profissionais de defesa cibernética selecionados. A ferramenta poderá auxiliar na identificação, validação e correção de vulnerabilidades em códigos. A proposta é ajudar equipes de segurança a encontrar problemas em softwares e desenvolver soluções para proteger sistemas. O acesso inicial será restrito a integrantes elegíveis do programa Fairwind, iniciativa voltada a profissionais de defesa cibernética. A novidade amplia a presença da IA nas atividades de segurança digital, área na qual a identificação rápida de falhas pode fazer diferença na proteção de sistemas e infraestruturas. Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

sources.name: SiliconANGLE
sources.title: Google’s latest midtier model Gemini 4 Neon is three times faster than Carbon and wins on some metrics
sources.text: After laying low during the summer while competitors Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC unleashed powerful new frontier models, Google LLC is hitting back. Having released its latest flagship model Gemini 4 Carbon one month ago, followed by the cost-effective Gemini 4 Hydrogen, it’s now striking a balance between the two with Gemini 4 Neon. Google announced its latest artificial intelligence offering in a blog post today, saying that Neon is a general-purpose model designed to handle complex coding tasks, multistep agentic workflows and analytical reasoning. Surprisingly, though Carbon is positioned as the company’s strongest model, Neon’s performance surpassed it on some tasks, according to benchmarks the company published today. Google also said Neon completes most tasks about three times as quickly as Carbon at costs of about 60% lower, making it “competitive with the leading models in its class.” Digging deeper into Google’s benchmarks, the company said Neon outranked the midtier Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.2 Sol models on tests such as knowledge work, reasoning, automation, multimodal understanding, cybersecurity, science and math. Those numbers were from Google’s own tests, but independent research by Artificial Analysis shows that Neon achieved an impressive score of 61 on the Intelligence Index, putting it third overall, just behind Anthropic’s most powerful model, Claude Fable 5.2, which scored 65, and OpenAI’s leading model GPT-6.2 Astra, which achieved a score of 62. Google continues to accelerate its release cadence with Gemini 4 Neon, delivering a small Intelligence gain over Gemini 4 Carbon at a ~17% lower Cost per Task @GoogleDeepMind has released Gemini 4 Neon, its fourth model in just seven weeks. Neon (xhigh) scores 61 on the… pic.twitter.com/L76oKwyxXa — Artificial Analysis (@ArtificialAnlys) November 18, 2026 With regard to cost, Neon isn’t quite so impressive. Google said it’s priced at a cost of $3 per million input tokens, 15 cents per million cached input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. That means it falls right in between GPT-6.2 Sol, which costs $2 per million input tokens, 10 cents per million cached tokens and $10 per million output tokens, and Claude Opus 5.5, which is priced at $4 per million input tokens, 20 cents per million cached tokens and $20 per million output tokens. Google’s choice of pricing is interesting because there’s a lot of debate around which model provider can achieve a genuine competitive advantage over its competitors. Given that these midtier models are so comparable in terms of performance, cost efficiency is becoming a more significant factor for enterprise customers. Although Neon appears to edge out GPT-6.2 Sol and Claude Fable 5.2 in terms of its ability to process several important workloads, many organizations might decide that’s not really enough to justify paying more to use it. Google said it’s making Neon available to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers from today in the Gemini application. Developers can also access it through the company’s paid application programming interface, the Google Antigravity platform and other business offerings. stories.title: How to Distill Gemini Into an Edge Model
stories.summary: Turn Gemini’s annotations into an edge model for manufacturing inspection. Explore three prompting approaches, review labels, and train RF-DETR model with Roboflow. Deploy the trained model near the camera and keep Gemini available to inspect difficult cases and improve future training data.

sources.name: Roboflow
sources.title: How to Distill Gemini Into an Edge Model
sources.text: To distill Gemini into an edge model, have Gemini label your images, review and correct those labels, then train a small detector that runs next to the camera and does the routine inspections. In Roboflow, auto-label with Gemini through a class description, the Auto Label agent or an Open Prompt Workflow. Then train RF-DETR Small on the reviewed dataset, run it with Inference on your edge device, and route uncertain cases back to Gemini or a human reviewer. Checking an assembly for missing screws takes more than counting detections. A model might miss one screw and mistake a reflection for another, returning the expected count while overlooking an incomplete product. A useful inspection system needs to locate the visible screws at each mounting position and flag images that need further review. With Roboflow, you can use Gemini to help build the training dataset for that system, then train a compact RF-DETR (opens in a new tab) model to detect screws near the camera. In this approach to model distillation , Gemini generates candidate bounding boxes, you review and correct the annotations, and RF-DETR learns the specific detection task. At deployment, the smaller model handles routine detection, while routing logic sends selected difficult images to Gemini or a person for review. In this guide, you’ll explore three ways to prompt Gemini for screw annotations: class descriptions in Roboflow Auto Label, conversational feedback with the Auto Label agent, and an Open Prompt Workflow that returns boxes for inspection in Python. You’ll then review the labels, train RF-DETR Small, test it on your edge hardware, and configure a fallback for uncertain results. Before generating labels, decide exactly what one object means. In our reference image, each screw annotation covers the full visible fastener region, including its outer exposed end and inner metal feature. One screw receives one box. This definition must stay the same across the dataset. Create an Object Detection project and upload the product images (opens in a new tab) . Include complete products, missing screws, reflections, and realistic changes in lighting. In Roboflow Auto Label , the class description is the prompt Gemini uses to find the object . Follow these steps. Gemini searches using that description, and Auto Label saves each resulting annotation as screw . The expected count of four is an application rule. It should not force the teacher to produce four boxes when a screw is missing. You can also describe the labeling task through Chat with Auto Label agent . The agent builds a labeling Workflow from the model and classes and shows a preview. Use the conversation to refine what it should label. The saved annotations still need a class name, which remains screw in this example. See labeling with the Auto Label agent (opens in a new tab) . With Gemini 4 Carbon selected, open Chat with Auto Label agent and enter the following request. Check the preview and request specific corrections. You can use the following correction when that error appears. You can also click an incorrect label or use Flag missing object. Once the preview matches the annotation rule, choose Use this Workflow, confirm the output-class mapping to screw , and select Label batch. Review the job estimate before starting. Continue with the label review in Section 2. This conversation configures the Auto Label Workflow. Gemini 4 Carbon remains the requested annotation model. Check that the saved Workflow uses it. Either setup option produces the same kind of training data for RF-DETR Small. The training examples contain reviewed screw bounding boxes. For this option, you can choose any Gemini model available in the Roboflow Google Gemini block (opens in a new tab) that supports image input and Open Prompt. You can also try different available models with the same prompt and images to compare their bounding boxes. For the Auto Label process above, Roboflow manages the saved annotations. Use the description field or the Auto Label agent conversation above. Neither option requires you to enter a JSON-format prompt or convert coordinates yourself. If you inspect raw Gemini detection output, Google's official object detection documentation (opens in a new tab) specifies box_2d in [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax] order, normalized to 0–1000. Normalization expresses a position relative to the image dimensions. A value of 500 is halfway across the relevant dimension, regardless of image size. Use the following conversion for an image of width W and height H. For example, [100, 200, 300, 250] on a 1000-pixel-wide, 600-pixel-high image gives pixel bounds xmin=200, ymin=60, xmax=250, ymax=180. This is a coordinate example, not a measured screw prediction. Prompting Gemini for boxes in a consistent format gives the visualization code a clear schema to check. Gemini models can still format their answers differently even when they receive the same instructions. This Open Prompt test uses a consistent box_2d schema and a model-independent parser. The prompt requests the screw label and [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax] coordinates normalized to 0–1000. The script accepts known JSON formatting differences, but checks the coordinates before drawing them. This follows Gemini’s object-detection coordinate convention (opens in a new tab) . The parser uses the requested coordinate order and scale. Numeric checks alone cannot prove that Gemini followed those instructions, so inspect the drawn boxes. Build this small test separately from Auto Label. Use an image input, a text input for the prompt, one Google Gemini block, and two outputs. Follow Build a Workflow (opens in a new tab) . Test with an assembly image and supply the example text in the Workflow’s prompt input. Confirm that both outputs, boxes_json and prompt_echo , appear in the test response. Save the Workflow and use Deploy (opens in a new tab) to copy its workspace slug, Workflow ID, and API URL for Python. Open Prompt returns raw text,

sources.name: ZDNet AI
sources.title: Google is making it easier to opt out of Gemini AI model training – here’s how
sources.text: You’ll soon be able to turn off Gemini model training but still retain access to your previous chats with Google’s AI. Google likes to use your conversations with Gemini for model training to help improve the AI. But for people with privacy concerns, the only way to opt out of this was to delete your entire chat history. Now, Google is overhauling the process to eliminate that drawback. Also: I checked Gemini’s new Memory summary to see what it knew about me In a change set to roll out in the coming weeks, you’ll be able to put the brakes on Gemini model training without losing access to your previous conversations with the AI. Here’s how this works now — and how it will work down the road. Currently, Gemini offers a setting called Keep Activity that controls not only whether and for how long your chats are saved but also whether they’re used to train the AI. You can’t separate the two. To correct this problem, Google will replace Keep Activity with two new settings. With the first setting, you’ll be able to keep or delete your past chats and choose how long your history will be saved. With the second setting, you’ll be able to decide whether your chats, including all text and attachments, will be used for model training. Also: I asked Gemini Notebook to ‘make me a site’ from my notes “With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training,” Google said in an announcement shared to Gemini users via email. Here’s how this will play out. If your Keep Activity setting is off when this change is made, both new settings will be off. If your Keep Activity setting is on, both new settings will be on. That means you’ll need to head to Gemini’s Settings if you wish to opt out of model training but still be able to view and access your previous chats. Almost all AIs include a setting for model training that you typically have to manually disable if you’re concerned about your privacy. But most let you opt out without turning off your chat history. ChatGPT offers a setting called “Improve the model for everyone,” which is double-speak for model training. But this is easy enough to turn off. Microsoft Copilot provides settings for “Training on conversation activity” and “Training on voice conversations,” both of which you can disable to opt out of model training. Claude’s AI training option is turned off by default. But you can always control this by checking the setting for “Help improve our AI models.” Also: 5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027 (Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.) In all those cases, you still retain access to your conversation history. In contrast, Google has been the only AI player among the majors to impose a restriction for those who want to opt out of AI training. Based on past actions, Google has often earned a reputation for being privacy-unfriendly. I’m glad to see the company take this step in the right direction. Last month it saved us real money after we got hit with a surprise $389 electric bill. My wife and I never would have caught that digging through the PDFs and emails ourselves. I use it for smaller stuff, too. For our upcoming holiday trip back to Oklahoma, I recently asked Gemini to give me the best options for a USB-C charger. Gemini quickly compared chargers thanks to Google’s Shopping Graph, asked me follow-up questions about the wattage and color, and then helped me check out using the new Google Pay integration. The best part: it also found a discount code so I saved an extra $10. Done. Gemini now uses the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) to make purchases like this. We’re working with American Express (coming soon), Mastercard, and Visa to keep your purchases secure with digital tokens on supported cards. And when you shop with Gemini, you still earn your card's points, cashback, or purchase protections during checkout. You can also set a hard spending cap upfront, and Gemini is designed to stay within your budget. All of your receipts and tracking info land straight in Google Wallet, which is expanding to iOS starting today . Up next, we’ll integrate the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) into Gemini so everyone can expect an even faster and more reliable shopping experience from discovery to checkout. Gemini lets you set the spending limit and still earn every airline mile, cashback point, and perk on your card. Gemini helps with weeknight dinners, too. I recently stared down a nearly empty fridge rushing out the door in the morning, and I texted Gemini with the new RCS integration 2 : “Add lasagna, strawberries, cucumbers, and vanilla ice cream to our Instacart order.” On the walk out, I saw an empty Cheerios box in the pantry, so I snapped a photo and sent a quick follow-up: “Add this too.” Gemini added it, and then handed me off to Instacart to complete the order. Groceries were on the doorstep when we got home. Done. Today, Gemini connects with more than 60 popular apps and, as a developer, you can apply to join our Connected Apps Platform . Earlier this week, I forwarded a batch of school emails from Gmail to gemini@google.com. In less than a minute, every date was on my calendar with my wife invited. sources.title: You can now see and edit what Google Gemini remembers about you
sources.text: Editing the AI’s memory is one way you can shape its responses. Besides the ability to connect and use other applications and services, a lot of AI assistants' utility comes from their capacity to shape their responses based on what they learn and remember about you. Google's Personal Intelligence feature allows Gemini to pull in context from Gmail, YouTube, Search and other Google apps, and the AI also builds out its memory based on your preferences and other personal facts that come up in chats . For example, if you share with Gemini that you're lactose intolerant, the bot will avoid recommending milk-based products. Depending on what you share, Gemini's picture of you can be fairly intimate, which makes the ability to edit the AI's memory all the more important. If you're curious about what Gemini knows or you want to edit what the AI can draw from to personalize its responses, Google is rolling out a way to see and change Gemini's memory directly from the settings menu. Google has two layers of settings for what you could call Gemini's memory, though the company only refers to one of them by that name. The first layer, the Keep Activity toggle, determines whether chats with Gemini are saved and associated with your Google Account. If you're 18 or older and you're logged into your personal account while using Gemini, the toggle is on by default. With Keep Activity enabled, whenever you sign in with your account you can pull up and re-engage past chats. If you disable it, chats won't be saved to your account, meaning they'll disappear after 72 hours and won't follow you across devices. The second layer is what Google actually calls the AI's Memory . Using the content of past chats, Gemini is able to build out a profile of you that it can reference to personalize its responses. The AI isn't able to create any memories unless it can remember and access your inputs, so Keep Activity needs to be on for this to work. If it is, you may notice Gemini taking your preferences and personal information into account in its responses. That's the AI's memory at work. If you're in the US, have a paid Google AI plan and memory is on, you can access Gemini's memory summary to see what it's compiled about you and edit this information to your liking. In the Gemini web app, click the Settings button (the gear icon) in the bottom left corner, click Personal Intelligence and then click Memory summary . Gemini will then generate a bulleted list of the major details it's gleaned about you, sorted into categories focused on things like your personal data, career information and various interests. It tends to know your pets' names, too. You can stop there if you only care about what Gemini knows, or you can tweak the AI's memory by clicking on the Edit button (the pen icon) in the top-right corner of the Memory summary window. In edit mode, any line in the summary can be rewritten or deleted, just like a Google Doc. If you'd prefer to prompt Gemini to make additions or subtractions, you can alternatively enter a prompt via the text box at the bottom of the window. Once you're happy with your changes, you can click Save to commit them to Gemini's memory. Gemini also saves a memory history of these changes and when they were made. So, while you can easily alter your personal timeline as it pertains to Gemini's reality, any adjustments will be tracked. If you'd prefer to turn off the memory system entirely rather than simply edit it, you can do so by clicking on the Memory toggle in the Personal Intelligence menu. Deselecting the toggle will stop Gemini from committing new facts to memory, but it doesn't delete old things it's learned. You can edit those details using the Memory summary, or delete chats completely from the Activity menu. To delete chats, head to the Gemini web app, click Settings and then select Activity . From the Activity menu, you can scroll through interactions you've had with Gemini by date and delete whichever ones you'd like by clicking on the "X" next to them. Deleting them removes those chats from the context pool that Gemini uses to personalize its responses. By combining all of these options, you can exert more control over what Google's AI knows and how it responds to your inputs, and ideally get more useful outputs in the process.

stories.title: Microsoft and organizations across industries launch AI Transparency Initiative to strengthen enterprise trust in AI models and agents
stories.summary: The post Microsoft and organizations across industries launch AI Transparency Initiative to strengthen enterprise trust in AI models and agents appeared first on Source .

sources.name: Microsoft Source
sources.title: Microsoft and organizations across industries launch AI Transparency Initiative to strengthen enterprise trust in AI models and agents
sources.text: REDMOND, Wash. — Nov. 17, 2026 — Organizations can observe much of the activity around AI models, but they often cannot reconstruct what happened between a request and an outcome, making it difficult to independently verify model behavior. At Microsoft Ignite on Tuesday, Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella announced the next phase of Microsoft’s commitment to making AI safer: the AI Transparency Initiative, a collaborative effort with customers and partners to establish a common, open approach to security and governance across models and providers. The initiative reflects a simple principle: Greater AI autonomy requires greater transparency. “For security controls to be effective, every organization needs greater transparency into the model itself,” said Hayete Gallot, Executive Vice President, Microsoft Security. “With this work, we will bring more transparency to all models. This is a critical step in making containment smarter and stronger, allowing us to better inform accountability and traceability.” Enterprises are connecting AI models to data, tools, credentials and infrastructure, enabling agents to take actions without human approval at every step. Existing controls can observe much of the activity around AI models, but they cannot see what happens within them or independently verify their accounts of their own behavior. This limits organizations’ ability to understand the context behind an agent’s actions. That evidence gap creates security, compliance, audit and accountability risk. Security teams need a new trust architecture to address the growing insider risks posed by increasingly capable AI agents. “As AI agents become more deeply integrated into enterprise operations, security teams need clear visibility into what those agents are accessing, what actions they’re taking and how those actions can be verified,” said Aanchal Gupta, Chief Security Officer, Adobe. “Building a common approach to AI transparency across the industry is essential to strengthening trust and helping organizations innovate with confidence while maintaining security and accountability.” The initiative has three parts. First, Microsoft will expand its participation in the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s SI Agent Standards Initiative and draw on its research to develop open, industrywide standards for AI transparency, security and governance. Second, Microsoft is collaborating with more than 40 organizations, including Accenture, Adobe, KPMG, Mastercard and Volvo Cars, to help develop open standards for AI systems that are accountable, independently verifiable and safe by design, regardless of the model or provider. Third, Microsoft will incorporate this work into Microsoft AI, Microsoft Foundry and Microsoft Copilot, enabling customers to use the resulting evidence with their security and compliance tools, whether from Microsoft or other providers. “Our clients want to move faster with AI, and they shouldn’t have to choose between innovation and safety,” said John Israel, Global Chief Information Security Officer, KPMG International. “Trust in AI requires transparency, explainability and responsible oversight. We’re proud to work with Microsoft on the AI Transparency Initiative to help establish open, industrywide standards that give organizations the visibility and control they need to deploy AI responsibly at scale.” Agents with access to data, tools and credentials carry the risk profile of a privileged insider but operate at machine speed and scale, making independent oversight essential. Accountability stays with the organization. When something consequential happens, leaders answer to customers, employees, boards, auditors and regulators. Blaming the AI isn’t an answer, and “trust the model” isn’t a control. The initiative is designed to work across models and providers, including closed and open-weight models, so developer teams can change or update the models powering their agents without compromising IT and security teams’ ability to govern them securely or compliance teams’ ability to audit their actions. “As organizations take the next step in their AI reinventions, they need a solid foundation of trust and confidence to build from,” said Harpreet Sidhu, global cybersecurity lead, Accenture. “Initiatives like this from Microsoft to take an open, industry-driven approach to AI transparency can help as we secure AI models and fit them with controls and governance. Accenture is proud to partner with Microsoft and other leaders in this space.” Microsoft believes every organization should be able to see what AI systems access and do, verify their actions independently and control what they are permitted to do. Organizations interested in helping shape the initiative or following its progress can learn more and sign up at aka.ms/learnmoreAItransparency . Follow the news from Microsoft Ignite, where Microsoft and industry leaders will share insights on how organizations can manage AI models and agents with confidence. sources.title: Introducing Roboflow Organizations for Enterprise
sources.text: Roboflow Organizations for Enterprise lets you roll vision AI out across departments and business units, while each team keeps its own Workspace, members, data and spending controls. Leaders get one dashboard for adoption and deployment volume, plus SSO, custom roles, export-control restrictions and credit reallocation across Workspaces. Over 80,000 organizations build with Roboflow, including teams at over half of the Fortune 100. Enterprises like Rivian, BNSF Railway , and USG use Roboflow to make visual intelligence part of their operations. Roboflow customers often begin with a small, nimble team deploying successful vision solutions using Roboflow, and want to quickly expand their solutions and Roboflow tooling across the rest of the enterprise without worrying about complex data and billing concerns. The most successful enterprises scale AI impact by ensuring that problems aren’t solved in silos, while retaining control, visibility, and delineation across teams. Today, we’re introducing Organizations. An Organization (opens in a new tab) brings multiple Workspaces together under one umbrella. Organizations let large enterprises scale vision AI capabilities across departments, units, and projects. Each Workspace keeps its own members, projects, data, internal spending controls, and access controls. Keeping those workspaces separate ensures teams within the organization can move quickly and adopt new capabilities without sacrificing organizational control and visibility. Most of the enterprises we work with ask: The Organization Dashboard answers those questions with a view of member activity, projects, deployment volume, and adoption trends across Workspaces. Often, enterprises have business units or teams subject to compliance or standards, whether from customers, internal policy, or because they operate in a regulated industry. Roboflow’s Enterprise controls include single sign-on, custom roles, folder permissions, and restrictions on access to export-controlled data. This means that a business unit handling regulated or commercially sensitive data can operate in a dedicated Workspace, with limited and controlled access, while not placing undue restrictions on other business units without such regulatory requirements. Leaders also need to understand credit usage and control spending. A dedicated page within the Organization Dashboard allows insight into where credits go across different departments, teams or units (organized by Workspace) and even more granularly into individual project folders. It supplies business leaders with the context necessary to allocate costs to sites and projects, plan next year’s use cases, and reallocate unused credits across Workspaces as team needs change. As enterprises expand their use of Roboflow, we’re making it easier to bring new teams onto the platform and manage access and usage across Workspaces. We will also be expanding Roboflow Organizations to support vendors that offer Roboflow-powered products to their own customers. Many enterprises already use Roboflow to build their company-wide vision program with Roboflow. Organization dashboards are available today on select enterprise workspaces. Please reach out to our team to get started rolling out vision AI to your organization.

sources.title: Microsoft unveiled Copilot Workspaces at Ignite 2026, plus more AI workplace updates
sources.text: The company also released new ROI tracking tools for companies monitoring their AI spend. AI-powered workspaces are tech companies’ latest focus, as the industry still struggles to perfect adoption. Microsoft has just put its offering into the ring. During the keynote for the company’s Ignite conference on Tuesday, CEO Satya Nadella announced Copilot Workspaces, a collaborative, “multiplayer” surface for Copilot’s agentic capabilities. Also: Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost The product, available in Frontier for now, is similar to OpenAI’s ChatGPT Space and several new Anthropic features, including Whiteboard and Sheets , which essentially merge the work tools you’re used to using with an agentic framework. “As the evolution of Copilot Notebooks, it’s where people and agents build on each other’s work,” Microsoft said. “An agent drafts a section of a document, and you review. You leave a comment, and an agent picks it up.” Microsoft also announced Autopilot , a sort of counterpoint agent to Copilot that “can watch Teams channels, follow up on emails, run recurring work, and manage a project — without waiting for a prompt,” as Microsoft described. In a demo video during the keynote, the agent appeared to function similarly to OpenAI’s Dots , but for work — employees can tag their Autopilot “like a colleague,” Microsoft said, and assign it tasks. Also: 4 ways Anthropic’s new Claude Sheets beat using a Google Sheets connector Microsoft said the agent will be able to autonomously handle “meetings and follow-ups on its own,” though that claim may be best verified by teams themselves. Speaking of trust, however, Microsoft noted that “Autopilot runs on the identity, security, and compliance foundation IT already uses,” and that “each Autopilot has its own Microsoft Entra Agent ID and a named manager,” meaning IT can block it as needed. “Its sign-ins and actions are logged under its own name, so security teams have a clear audit trail. Powered by Work IQ, it understands how your organization works within existing permissions,” Microsoft said. The company added that employees will soon “be able to bring their personal Autopilot into Workspaces” as well. The feature is also available in Frontier. Nadella also announced a few other productivity features, including a “command center” called Today that spans email, calendar, meetings, tasks, and threads in Teams. Currently in private preview in Outlook and the Copilot app, it includes a personalized briefing and a feed of priorities that updates throughout the day. “The draft is written and ready for you to edit; the schedule change is already proposed; and the forgotten follow-up is waiting for you to send it, complete with context so you can catch up quickly,” Microsoft said of the feature, which sounds like an agentic briefing-cum-morning-assistant. Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill Microsoft also announced that Home, now generally available, unifies Chat and Cowork into a singular starting point. That’s similar to Anthropic’s recent consolidation of its chat and agentic Cowork offerings, demonstrating an overall trend toward simplification in workplace AI. While more companies are finally starting to see a return on their AI investment, agents are still expensive and can quickly rack up costs when unsupervised. Microsoft announced a few tools to track this at Ignite: Agent 365 Business Analytics and Agent 365 Cost Management. Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math? Agent 365, which Microsoft announced last year, is the company’s observability platform. Microsoft said Business Analytics, in Frontier Public today, provides insights on what a company is spending on AI and why, and where it’s paying off, as well as forecasts future costs. In a demo during the keynote, Microsoft showed how admins can see when specific agents’ costs have spiked recently and what (human) employee to notify as a result. “It starts with a new way to measure your investment: in work completed, not simply tokens,” Microsoft said. “It analyzes the tasks, how long that work typically takes a person, and the share Cowork performed, providing a sophisticated view of the hours your intelligence supports and what the work is worth.” Cost Management lets IT see where teams are using AI down to the model. “Leaders can set spending policies, limits, and proactive alerts and control which models are available,” Microsoft said. Anthropic released a similar tool last month, though it was focused more on making seats as efficient as possible on Teams and Enterprise plans. sources.title: At Ignite 2026, Microsoft reinvents Copilot as the autonomous engine of enterprise work
sources.text: Business knowledge workers spend their days running a gauntlet of emails, spreadsheets, messaging platforms, meetings and productivity applications, wasting hours of their time switching from one to another to get mundane tasks done. Microsoft Corp. is now proposing an alternative: It wants Copilot to evolve from a somewhat useful generative artificial intelligence assistant into the autonomous foundation for all business work. At Microsoft Ignite 2026 today in San Francisco, it unveiled a slate of powerful new capabilities and features for its favorite autonomous tool as part of its ongoing effort to transform Copilot into the new workplace operating system. The company’s new vision was outlined in a blog post by Microsoft Chief Marketing Officer Jared Spataro, who pointed to its comprehensive intelligence layer for work, called WorkIQ , as the critical engine behind this shift. Spataro explained that enterprise work is notoriously messy. Microsoft 365 stores roughly 19.5 exabytes of customer’s business data, and it’s adding billions of new files, documents, emails and messages each day. For businesses, it’s not enough to just give an autonomous AI agent access to this data and expect it to start making sense of it. It needs WorkIQ, which acts as the centralized reasoning layer for all Copilot agents, retrieving data, understanding its intent, identifying what’s important for the task it has been assigned while ignoring everything else. While WorkIQ sits under the hood, Spataro says, the average worker’s day will soon begin in “ Home ,” which is the new user interface for Copilot. Home merges traditional chat with a portal called Cowork , which is where people can start delegating different tasks to AI agents. Spataro said Home is like a grounding anchor, or a place where workers can log in each day to pick up where they left off. Home’s key element is Auto, which is an intelligent composer that dynamically routes users’ requests and prompts to the most suitable AI model. It’s the place where most people will typically begin each new task. “Tell Copilot what you want to accomplish and it intelligently routes the work to the right models and effort for the task,” Spataro explained. “For more complex work, Auto may recommend moving from Chat to Cowork. If you agree, Copilot transfers the tasks seamlessly, helping to deliver the outcome with the right level of investment.” Another key part of Home is called Today. It’s a “proactive command center” that’s currently available in private preview that scans a user’s email, calendar and Teams threads in order to highlight the things they have to get done that day. Best of all, it won’t leave users feeling overwhelmed, Spataro said, because it also helps them to complete that work. For instance, it can quickly draft replies to emails, propose alterations to someone’s schedule and queue other messages for the user to review. Copilot’s ability to get work done has been advanced by its deeper integration with Microsoft’s Office suite. Spataro said the company is bringing the full capabilities of Office directly into the Copilot application. As a result, users will be able to move effortlessly from ideation on a notepad or whiteboard to conjure up a completed Word document or Excel spreadsheet based on what they just outlined. Those files will live entirely within Copilot, which gains the ability to co-author alongside human colleagues. Because Office is now native to Copilot, every document and file will be secured by Microsoft 365’s strict security and compliance controls, Spataro said. Human-to-agent collaboration is being boosted too with the arrival of Copilot Workspaces, which is a kind of canvas that both can access, Spataro said. Within Copilot Workspaces, an agent might draft a section of a document, then notify a human to come and review it when they get the chance. The human will be able to leave comments for other agents to address. Further aiding Copilot in work automation is a new capability called Autopilot , which dramatically enhances what the tool can now do. Autopilot is available now to subscribers who have enrolled in Microsoft’s Frontier early-access program. It’s a fully autonomous and always-on AI agent that comes with its own Microsoft Entra identity, memory and an ecosystem of productivity tools. Autopilot is very different from standard AI agents that are programmed to wait for a user’s prompts. It’s continuously available, watching various Teams channels and the user’s email inbox for updates. It can automate recurring work processes, and it can manage entire project pipelines, such as a multistep supplier review, fully autonomously, Spataro said. Autopilot is powerful, but safeguards are in place. Information technology teams have complete control over what it can and can’t access, and if something goes wrong they can step in and block it from doing anything else at a moment’s notice. “Its sign-ins and actions are logged under its own name, so security teams have a clear audit trail,” Spataro explained. “Powered by WorkIQ, it understands how your organization works within existing permissions. You decide what work Autopilot takes on and it will always check with you before key actions.” Coding continues to be a major focus, and now Microsoft is giving everyday knowledge workers the ability to build software that can help them get their work done even faster. With Copilot Code , launching in a few week’s time, users will be able to generate interactive dashboards, persistent desktop widgets and lightweight business applications from simple, natural language prompts. All of these Copilot-generated apps will be hosted within Copilot Managed Runtime , which is a new, highly-secure environment that IT teams can monitor to ensure none of them pose a risk to the company’s data. To reassure organizations that their AI agents are not only secure, but also providing real value, Microsoft has updated the Agent 365 platform to give
